points.description: Every step is valid and the final count is correct for the given value of T. Key condition: with BC = T and angle B = 30°, two triangles (two values of AB) exist exactly when T·sin30° < AC < T, i.e. T/2 < AC < T (strict at both ends: AC = T/2 gives one right-angle triangle, AC = T gives one triangle, AC < T/2 gives none). The answer is the number of integers strictly between T/2 and T. For integer T this is ceil(T/2) − 1 (T even: T/2 − 1; T odd: (T−1)/2). Equivalent reasoning (law of cosines giving AB² − T√3·AB + T² − AC² = 0 with two distinct positive roots) is acceptable. The final number must match the count for the T supplied; wrong endpoint inclusion (e.g. counting AC = T/2 or AC = T) or a wrong count earns 0.

rubric.notes: Full mark only for a fully valid argument (condition T/2 < AC < T, strict) and the correct integer count for the T in use. Any invalid step, wrong inequality, or wrong final count earns 0. There are no part marks.
rubric.answer_key: Ambiguous case (SSA): fix BC = T and angle B = 30°. The distance from C to line AB is T·sin30° = T/2. Two triangles occur iff T/2 < AC < T. Check with the law of cosines: AC² = AB² + T² − √3·T·AB, so AB² − √3·T·AB + (T² − AC²) = 0. Two distinct positive roots need discriminant 3T² − 4(T² − AC²) > 0, i.e. AC > T/2, and a positive product T² − AC² > 0, i.e. AC < T. So the answer is the number of integers strictly between T/2 and T, which is ceil(T/2) − 1 for integer T. Examples: T = 12 gives 7..11, so 5; T = 11 gives 6..10, so 5. T is not given (TNYWR), so substitute the actual value.
